content.text:
**BIS Hanoi has a strong reputation.** It's generally seen as one of the top British-curriculum schools in the city, with good exam results, proper accreditation and good facilities. It's also one of the more expensive schools. Whether it's worth it for your child mostly depends on cost, the commute, and the kind of school community you want.

**Strengths**

- **Exam results:** Its students consistently do well on the IB Diploma, the two-year programme taken in the final years of school.
The Class of 2026 averaged 35.11 points, well above the global average of 30.88.
The school says this is
the ninth year in a row it has beaten the worldwide average.
In 2025 the average was lower, at
, but still above average. These figures come from the school's own announcements, but independent reviewers report the same numbers. At IGCSE (the exams taken around age 16), the school reports
46% of grades at A* to A, compared with 23% in England.
- **Accreditation and ownership:**
The school was re-accredited by the Council of International Schools in January 2024.
It's owned by Nord Anglia, which also lists accreditation from WASC (a US accrediting body) and FOBISIA membership.

Nord Anglia is a large global group of private schools, so the school is well funded and well organised.
- **Independent reviews:** The Good Schools Guide describes it as
"a lively school that straddles the feel of a British state school with the high educational standards and unmatched facilities of a privately funded school."
- **Popularity with parents:**
It was named in the Top 10 in Vietnam in the Edarabia Parents' Choice Awards 2026, which are based on parent reviews.

The school publicises this itself.

**Things to check before deciding**

- **Fees:**
For 2025/2026, annual tuition ranges from VND 329.9 million to VND 932.8 million depending on the year group

(roughly US$13,000–37,000). Fees go up sharply in the senior years, so plan for the full time your child will be there.
- **Who the other students are:** The Good Schools Guide notes that
Vietnamese parents like that their children will largely be with other children of a

Vietnamese background. Many students are Vietnamese. That's an advantage if you want strong local ties. If you're an expat family hoping for a very mixed international group, UNIS Hanoi (which teaches the IB from the start) is the usual alternative.
- **Teacher turnover:** Staff reviews on Glassdoor are mixed. One former employee complained that
"young, inexperienced staff are hired yearly"

, and others mention heavy workloads. That's only 5 reviews, so don't read too much into it. Still, ask the school how long teachers usually stay.
- **Location:** The school is in
Vinhomes Riverside, Long Bien District

. Some websites wrongly say it's in Tay Ho or that it offers A-Levels. It's across the river from Tay Ho, where many expats live, so test the commute at rush hour.
- **Curriculum:** It follows the British system through IGCSE, then the IB Diploma for the final two years, not A-Levels. That's a good fit if you're aiming for UK or international universities.

**My view:** It's a safe, well-regarded choice if you want a British-style education with good results and can afford the fees. Before committing, visit and ask about:

- how long teachers usually stay
- class sizes in your child's year group
- the mix of nationalities in that year
- support for English learners or special needs, if relevant
- where recent graduates went to university

It's also worth comparing it with UNIS, BVIS (Nord Anglia's cheaper bilingual school) and Hanoi Academy. If you tell me your child's age, nationality, budget and which universities you're aiming for, I can help you narrow it down.
